title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models
authors: Aravindan Kamatchi Sundaram, B. Pabitramohan Prusty, Rohit Batra
abstract: Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

infographic.key_insight: This review traces how materials information extraction has evolved from rule-based pipelines to multimodal LLMs and agentic systems that support materials discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated literature extraction can populate materials databases and knowledge graphs to support research assistance and, when integrated with autonomous laboratories, closed-loop optimization.
method: Review rule-based, NLP, transformer-encoder, and LLM extraction approaches.
Examine extraction across text, tables, and figures.
Assess generated datasets, extraction accuracy, computational costs, and pipeline design.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a critical assessment of datasets and extraction methods but provides no numerical accuracy or cost results and highlights scarce reliable benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Reliable sample-level linking of structure, properties, processing, and performance remains an open challenge, complicated by inconsistent terminology across document modalities.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Materials Data and Knowledge Extraction using Machine Learning and Large Language Models

title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery
authors: Yazhuo Liu, Kunqing Ding, Xiaoguo Gong, Zifeng Wang, Yichen Yang, Yifeng Che
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems hold immense potential for automating complex workflows in materials discovery and design, but extending them to domain-intensive mechanistic investigations remains challenging. Here, we present GBClaw, an agentic AI framework for investigating the structure and deformation of general grain boundaries (GBs). Although general GBs constitute the vast majority of real-world interfaces in polycrystalline materials, they remain understudied because their structural complexity and interfacial mismatch complicate experimental and modeling research. GBClaw integrates large language models (LLMs) into a modular architecture comprising an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain-specific tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory. Through dynamic replanning and iterative workflow refinement, the framework effectively connects systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis. Applied to 14 general asymmetric tilt GBs in nickel, GBClaw characterized interfacial defect structures and identified diverse deformation modes across these incommensurate boundaries. Comparing boundary sliding with and without secondary GB misfit dislocations revealed substantial differences in shear strength, underscoring the critical role of defect hierarchies in sliding resistance. Furthermore, researcher-guided follow-up calculations traced an anomalously high shear resistance to metastable boundary structures. This work demonstrates that combining agentic AI with domain expertise bridges high-throughput computational screening with deep physical understanding of complex material interfaces.

infographic.key_insight: GBClaw connects agentic AI-driven simulations with mechanistic analysis, revealing how defect hierarchies and metastable grain-boundary structures influence sliding resistance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding deformation at general grain boundaries can inform microstructure design aimed at controlling interfacial strength in polycrystalline materials.
method: Integrate LLMs with an orchestrator, specialized agents, domain tools, simulation interfaces, and hierarchical memory.
Use dynamic replanning to connect systematic simulations with targeted mechanistic analysis.
Compare sliding with and without secondary grain-boundary misfit dislocations, then investigate anomalies through researcher-guided calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 14 general asymmetric tilt grain boundaries in nickel, GBClaw identified diverse deformation modes and substantial shear-strength differences associated with secondary misfit dislocations.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to the studied nickel boundaries, and investigation of anomalous resistance required researcher-guided follow-up.
infographic.paper_title: GBClaw: An agentic AI framework for atomistic grain boundary research and mechanistic discovery

title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films
authors: K. Starkey, L. Kahle, M. Christensen, V. Eyert, A. El-Azab, C. B. Geller
abstract: A first-principles-informed multiscale modeling approach is reported for oxide formation during corrosion of zirconium. The present simulations reproduce the columnar corrosion film microstructure and grain size distribution seen in micrographs of oxidized Zr surfaces. This structural feature emerges from a hexagonal ZrO layer adjacent to the $α$-Zr/ZrO$_{2-x}$ interface, which is dynamically stabilized by continuous heterogeneous grain nucleation and grain boundary mass diffusion. This ZrO layer is identified as a significant oxygen diffusion barrier and a potential contributor to sub-parabolic pretransition corrosion kinetics. The simulations also reproduce the undulatory nature of the metal/oxide interface, leading to regions with tensile stress components capable of nucleating cracks, despite the overall state of compressive hydrostatic stress within the oxide film. First principles density functional theory (DFT) computations of fundamental ZrO$_x$ properties were combined with molecular dynamics simulations using a machine-learned potential based on a DFT training set to provide extensive input to an advanced phase field model for oxide formation and its microstructure, as implemented in the new MedeA PhaseField module. The phase field simulations reported herein incorporated computed stoichiometry-dependent thermochemical data, anisotropic elastic properties, interface energies, bulk and grain boundary mass transport processes, multiphase heterogeneous grain nucleation, and strain energy-dependent phase stabilities.

infographic.key_insight: Multiscale simulations identify a dynamically sustained hexagonal ZrO interlayer that helps explain columnar oxide microstructures and may slow oxygen transport during zirconium corrosion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting oxide morphology, oxygen transport barriers, and local tensile stresses could improve assessments of zirconium corrosion and crack initiation.
method: Compute ZrOₓ thermochemistry, elasticity, and interface properties using DFT.
Use DFT-trained machine-learned molecular dynamics to supply additional material inputs.
Simulate oxide growth with a phase-field model coupling diffusion, heterogeneous nucleation, and strain-dependent phase stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations reproduce columnar oxide morphology and grain-size distributions observed in micrographs, as well as an undulating metal/oxide interface.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation errors or direct kinetic measurements confirming the proposed ZrO barrier's contribution to sub-parabolic corrosion.
infographic.paper_title: Multiscale Modeling of Zr Corrosion: Predicting Microstructures of Oxide Films

title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites
authors: Can Erer, H. Birkan Yilmaz, Nebahat Aral
abstract: Evaluating the energy transmission ratio of an X-ray beam through a polymer composite is a challenging task in radiation shielding studies. The reference solution with Monte Carlo transport simulation is highly accurate but computationally expensive: each of our reference simulations is capped at $4\times10^9$ photon histories and a 20,000 s (over 5 hours) time limit, while closed-form analytical methods fail to represent such complex scenarios. We present an artificial neural network model that maps the unordered multi-set of molecular constituents, their mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors directly to the transmission ratio $I(t)/I_0$ in 1-3 milliseconds. The model is a Set Transformer, which makes it permutation invariant by construction and accepts mixtures of different sizes up to 11 constituents within a fixed-size padded set. Each constituent is embedded with a chemistry-pretrained transformer language model, ChemBERTa. In our proposed method, training data are produced by an automated PENELOPE/penEasy pipeline using the radiation source at 30, 80, 100, and 120 kV tube voltages over polyethylene-based shielding composite slabs of thicknesses spanning 0.15-2.5 mm. After preprocessing, the dataset contains $n = 4697$ simulated configurations on which a leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation is performed, attaining mean squared error MSE = $(1.12 \pm 0.56)\times10^{-4}$, normalized-MSE percentage NMSE% = 0.0294% $\pm$ 0.0147%, and $R^2 = 0.9988$. The corresponding per-sample percentage errors give an alpha-trimmed ($α= 0.10$) absolute percentage error (APE) of 1.66% and a median APE of 1.15%. Our model's inference is several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying Monte Carlo simulation (sub-millisecond per query vs. several hours for the reference run) with effective accuracy in predicting $I(t)/I_0$.

infographic.key_insight: STAR-XPC predicts X-ray transmission through polymer composites in milliseconds, closely matching computationally expensive Monte Carlo simulations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could accelerate screening of polyethylene-based radiation shields across composition, thickness, and X-ray source settings.
method: Embed molecular constituents with pretrained ChemBERTa.
Combine constituent embeddings, mass fractions, and four bulk physical descriptors.
Use a permutation-invariant Set Transformer supporting up to 11 constituents to predict I(t)/I₀.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 4,697 simulated configurations, leakage-free, jointly stratified 10-fold cross-validation achieved R² = 0.9988 and median absolute percentage error of 1.15%.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the simulated polyethylene-based composites, 0.15–2.5 mm thickness range, and four tested tube voltages remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: STAR-XPC: Set Transformer for Estimating X-ray Transmission in Polymer Composites

title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys
authors: Daniil M. Khodachenko, Andrei V. Ruban, Franco Moitzi, Oleg E. Peil, Vsevolod I. Razumovskiy
abstract: The atomic ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys strongly influences their magnetic properties and mechanical behavior. While general features of long-range atomic ordering are known from the experimentally established phase diagram in this composition range, detailed atomic configurations and driving forces behind them remain speculative. Here, we address this gap by using effective cluster interactions (ECI) obtained from density functional theory (DFT) calculations and subsequent statistical thermodynamics modeling to unravel the interplay between magnetism, composition, and temperature in body-centered cubic (bcc) Fe-Si alloys up to 20 at% Si. Our analysis reveals that the ordering behavior is governed by a strong coupling between magnetic order, lattice expansion, and Si concentration, with specific ECI shells switching sign or magnitude as the magnetic state changes, which is reflected in the phase equilibria and ordering behavior of Fe-Si alloys. In particular, we demonstrate that D0$_3$ ordering is, in fact, primary in the totally ordered ferromagnetic state, while the B2 type of ordering is promoted in the paramagnetic state at elevated temperatures. The temperature-dependent evolution of these ordering patterns, obtained from Monte Carlo simulations based on the magnetically resolved ECIs, reproduces the experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range order characteristics. By explicitly linking the magnetic state with the effective interactions and macroscopic phase behavior, this work establishes a predictive framework for an ab initio-based description of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys and highlights the decisive role of magnetism in ordering phenomena in this system.

infographic.key_insight: Magnetism reshapes atomic ordering in Fe-rich Fe–Si alloys: D0₃ ordering dominates in the fully ordered ferromagnetic state, while B2 ordering is promoted in the elevated-temperature paramagnetic state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linking magnetic state to atomic ordering can help guide composition and thermal-processing choices for Fe–Si alloys whose magnetic and mechanical properties depend on atomic arrangement.
method: Compute effective cluster interactions from density functional theory for bcc Fe–Si alloys up to 20 at% Si.
Resolve how magnetic state, lattice expansion, and Si concentration alter these interactions.
Use Monte Carlo simulations to predict temperature-dependent ordering and phase behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that simulations reproduce experimentally observed phase equilibria and short-range order characteristics, but provides no quantitative accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Predictions are demonstrated for bcc alloys up to 20 at% Si; use beyond this range requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: First-principles modeling of ordering in Fe-rich Fe-Si alloys

title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction
authors: Adam Zheng, April Zheng, Sheng Ran
abstract: AI/ML models are useful for the prediction of materials' properties. Recently, there has been great progress in developing Neural Network models to predict the properties of solids, molecules, and crystals, avoiding expensive and time-consuming laboratory testing. This study presents a novel AI/ML-based multi-modal approach to predict material magnetic ordering using material crystal structure information as input to a Graph Neural Network model (GNN) and semantic text descriptions of the material's properties and structure as input to a Large Language Model (LLM), before performing information fusion of the GNN and LLM outputs to predict material magnetic ordering in four classes (Non-magnetic, Ferromagnetic, Antiferromagnetic, Ferrimagnetic). The model is trained, validated, and tested on a dataset which is a combination of Materials Project dataset, Magndata dataset, and a set of uranium compounds with magnetic ordering determined in laboratory testing, with an 80/10/10 (training/validation/testing) data split. The proposed GNN and LLM multi-modal approach achieves better overall accuracy than both the standalone GNN and LLM approaches with three fusion strategies.

infographic.key_insight: Combining crystal-structure GNN outputs with material-description LLM outputs improves magnetic-ordering classification over either model alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support computational screening of magnetic materials before expensive laboratory characterization.
method: Encode crystal structures with a graph neural network.
Process semantic descriptions of material properties and structure with a large language model.
Fuse model outputs using three strategies to classify non-magnetic, ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic, or ferrimagnetic ordering.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation uses combined Materials Project, Magndata, and laboratory-characterized uranium-compound data with an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split; the abstract reports higher overall accuracy for multimodal fusion but gives no numerical scores.
infographic.watch_item: Check that text descriptions exclude magnetic-ordering labels or proxies that could leak the prediction target.
infographic.paper_title: Crystal Structure Based Graph Neural Network And LLM Multi-Modal Approach for Material Magnetic Ordering Prediction

title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons
authors: Joseph Hart, Samuel G. H. Brookes, Fabian L. Thiemann, Christoph Schran
abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise broad transferability, yet their out-of-domain reliability is hard to establish. Here, we use pure and O/H-containing disordered carbon spanning multiple phases, competing hybridisations and porous frameworks to stress-test six popular foundation MLIPs. We first screen all six on density functional theory (DFT) energy and force errors and binding curves, then subject four to melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics and evaluate the resulting structural observables. Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories reveal unphysical extrapolation and dynamical failures that low DFT energy and force errors fail to reveal. Of the models tested, MACE-MH-1 is the most consistently robust, with low DFT errors and stable MD. Despite differing architectures, OMAT-based models share structural biases, highlighting the importance of training coverage. All four models generate structures of nanoporous carbon that reproduce the principal experimental and specialised carbon potential signatures. Incorporating O/H leaves short-range order largely unchanged but shifts pore-size distributions towards larger pores. These results emphasise the need for application-specific validation and extend molecular dynamics modelling of nanoporous carbon towards experimentally realistic structures.

infographic.key_insight: Low DFT prediction errors do not guarantee reliable dynamics in disordered carbon; MACE-MH-1 was the most consistently robust foundation potential tested.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Foundation potentials can support nanoporous-carbon modelling, but application-specific stability and structural validation are essential before deployment.
method: Screened six foundation MLIPs using DFT energy and force errors plus binding curves.
Tested four models with melt-quench-anneal molecular dynamics.
Evaluated structural observables in pure and O/H-containing disordered carbons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Binding curves and O/H-containing trajectories exposed failures missed by low DFT errors, while all four MD-tested models reproduced principal nanoporous-carbon signatures.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness remains application-dependent: OMAT-based models shared structural biases despite differing architectures, highlighting training-coverage concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Challenging Atomistic Foundation Models on Disordered Carbons

title: Instability-driven segregation of V group transition metals on HEB$_2$ grain boundaries influencing enhanced mechanical properties
authors: Daniil Alekseev, Viktor S. Baidyshev, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: Five metals share a common sublattice in the (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B$_2$ (HEB$_2$). Most high-entropy materials are produced as polycrystalline materials in the form of sintered ceramics. The question of which metal species are located at grain boundaries is still unknown. Here, we calculated the grain-boundary energy $γ_{GB}$ of four types of boundaries in five binary diborides and HEB$_2$ using density functional theory (DFT). We analyzed the bonding at these boundaries using COHP and sampled cation segregation at six boundaries of HEB$_2$, ordered and general, using Monte Carlo / molecular dynamics with a MACE potential that was fine-tuned for this system. According to our results $γ_{GB}$ splits by group: the group V diborides NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$ form boundaries with about half the energy of the group IV at three of the four types of GBs, ranging from 0.8 to 2.7 compared to 2.5--4.8~J/m$^2$. COHP shows a significant difference at the Fermi level, namely the Me--B bonds of NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$ are antibonding at Fermi energy ($E_F$) in the bulk but bonding at the GB, while their integrated strength hardly changes. In HEB$_2$ the segregation follows a similar pattern: Nb and Ta are enriched at five of the six grain boundaries, including general boundaries, up to 23--35~at.\% at 2000~K, although the size of the atoms would favor Zr and Hf in the expanded sites. A segregated $Σ193$ grain boundary can withstand 26 against 20~GPa for a random boundary in tension at 300~K. The grain boundaries of HEB$_2$ are composed of group V metals, as suggested by the boundary energies of binaries compounds and their bonding at the Fermi level. Grain boundaries of the (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B$_2$ preferentially include Nb and Ta. This lowers the grain boundary energy and strengthens the boundaries. This consists of the lower boundary energy and changes Fermi level bonding in NbB$_2$ and TaB$_2$.

infographic.key_insight: Nb and Ta preferentially segregate to (Hf,Ta,Ti,Nb,Zr)B₂ grain boundaries, linking lower boundary energies and favorable Fermi-level bonding to stronger interfaces.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling grain-boundary chemistry could improve the mechanical performance of high-entropy diboride ceramics.
method: DFT calculations of four grain-boundary types in five binary diborides and HEB₂.
COHP analysis of metal–boron bonding at grain boundaries.
Monte Carlo/molecular dynamics sampling of six HEB₂ boundaries using a fine-tuned MACE potential.
infographic.evidence_signal: Nb and Ta enriched at five of six HEB₂ boundaries to reported concentrations of 23–35 at.% at 2000 K; a segregated Σ193 boundary sustained 26 GPa versus 20 GPa for a random boundary at 300 K.
infographic.watch_item: The computational findings require experimental validation, and the reported strength gain for one boundary may not generalize to bulk polycrystalline ceramics.
infographic.paper_title: Instability-driven segregation of V group transition metals on HEB$_2$ grain boundaries influencing enhanced mechanical properties

title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition
authors: Mingxuan Chen, Chao Chen, Siqi Jiang, Shuxiang Qiao, Hongyan Lu, Di Zhang
abstract: The iron-based ferromagnetic materials have emerged as a promising system for spintronics due to their high Curie temperatures and significant anomalous Hall effect (AHE) driven by Berry curvature. While there have been investigations into the epitaxial growth of non-layered iron-based ferromagnetic materials, the realization of high-quality single crystal thin films continues to be a formidable obstacle. Meanwhile, the issues such as grain boundary scattering further hinder their characterization and application. Here, we report the first chemical vapor deposition (CVD) synthesis of single-crystalline cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge nanoplates. This compound represents a substantial departure from the conventional hexagonal phases typically observed in the Fe-Ge system. Structural characterizations confirm the cubic lattice and stoichiometric purity of the crystals. Structural analysis identifies a strong epitaxial effect, resulting in a giant compressive strain of ~4.16% at the interface that relaxes gradually toward the surface. The second-harmonic generation (SHG) signals might further reveal that such interfacial strain disrupted the inherent centro-symmetry of the cubic phase. SQUID magnetometry shows robust room-temperature ferromagnetism and clear magnetic anisotropy. Magneto-transport measurements reveal a robust AHE that remains stable at temperatures far exceeding room temperature. The scaling observed between the anomalous Hall resistance and longitudinal resistance strongly suggests that this effect is dominated by the intrinsic Berry curvature mechanism. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the huge epitaxial strain induces band reconstructions and creates dense spin-orbit coupling gaps near the Fermi level, effectively doubling the anomalous Hall conductivity to match our experimental observations.

infographic.key_insight: CVD-grown single-crystalline cubic D0₃-Fe₃Ge nanoplates exhibit robust anomalous Hall behavior, with calculations linking epitaxial strain to enhanced Berry-curvature-driven conductivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These epitaxial ferromagnetic nanoplates offer a potential platform for spintronic devices operating above room temperature.
method: CVD synthesis and structural characterization of cubic D0₃-Fe₃Ge nanoplates.
SQUID magnetometry, magnetotransport, and second-harmonic generation measurements.
DFT calculations of strain-induced band reconstruction and anomalous Hall conductivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Structural analysis indicates ~4.16% interfacial compressive strain; transport scaling supports an intrinsic AHE mechanism, while DFT predicts roughly doubled anomalous Hall conductivity consistent with experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Strain relaxes toward the surface, making thickness-dependent strain control an important concern for reproducible device integration.
infographic.paper_title: Robust Anomalous Hall Effect in Epitaxial Cubic D0$_3$-Fe$_3$Ge Nanoplates Grown by Chemical Vapor Deposition

title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires
authors: Yasir Mahmood, Daniel Wines, Viviana Dovale-Farelo, Kamal Choudhary, Lucas M Hale
abstract: Silicon nanowires (Si NWs) have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation nanoelectronic devices due to their tunable electronic properties, and compatibility with aggressive scaling requirements. The integration of strain further enhances their performance by modulating carrier mobility, band structure, and transport behavior without altering material chemistry. Within the NW, the silicon-silicon dioxide (Si-SiO$_{2}$) interface serves as a critical region where strain redistribution and suboxide bonding collectively influence the mechanical and electronic response. Here, we combine reactive force field molecular dynamics and first-principles calculations to investigate how oxidation-induced interfacial structure and crystallographic facet orientation govern strain-dependent bond evolution and facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties in oxidized Si NWs. Simulated dry thermal oxidation generates chemically realistic Si-SiO$_{2}$ interfaces, enabling direct characterization of bond order redistribution and stress gradient development across the interface under tensile strain. Interfacial Si-Si bonds exhibit elongation and reduced bond order associated with partial oxidation states, leading to localized stress concentration and preferential bond rupture. Complementary density functional theory calculations on facet-specific models reveal that orientation-dependent interfacial bonding modulates facet-dependent strain response of electronic properties. Together, these results establish a direct coupling between interfacial suboxide chemistry, mechanical deformation, and electronic structure, providing atomistic insight into strain-modulated behavior at oxidized silicon interfaces in faceted NWs.

infographic.key_insight: Interfacial suboxide chemistry couples tensile strain to bond weakening and localized stress in oxidized silicon nanowires, while facet orientation shapes the electronic response to strain.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling interface chemistry and crystallographic facets could help tune strain-sensitive nanoelectronic behavior while managing mechanical weak points.
method: Simulate dry thermal oxidation using reactive force field molecular dynamics.
Track interfacial bond evolution and stress gradients under tensile strain.
Use density functional theory on facet-specific models to assess electronic response.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show elongated, lower-bond-order interfacial Si–Si bonds associated with partial oxidation and preferential rupture, alongside facet-dependent electronic responses in first-principles calculations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational findings without experimental validation or quantified device-level performance gains.
infographic.paper_title: Strain-Induced Interfacial Bond Evolution and Facet-dependent Strain Response of Electronic Properties in Oxidized Silicon Nanowires

title: Polymer-Mediated Hotspot Evolution in Shock-Induced Pore Collapse in 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX)-based Explosives
authors: Jalen Macatangay, Brenden W. Hamilton, Alejandro Strachan
abstract: The initiation of detonation in high explosives (HEs) under shock loading is strongly influenced by the collapse of porosity and the subsequent formation of hotspots. As these materials are widely integrated with polymer binders to form polymer-bonded explosives, the collapse of pores at explosive-binder interfaces has received significant interest. Recent molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed that the shock-driven expansion of soft polymers (e.g. polystyrene) into a void produces greater pressure-volume (PV) work during recompression and higher local temperatures compared to pore collapse in neat HEs, ultimately expediting the onset of chemical reactions. Yet how pore collapse, interfacial phenomena, and binder chemistry jointly affect initiation remains insufficiently understood. We provide deeper insights into the role of polymer in hotspot evolution through reactive MD simulations, specifically characterizing its chemical behavior during the shock-induced collapse of voids at sizes approaching experimentally relevant length scales. We consider the HE 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX) in a crystal-gap-crystal stack with polystyrene along the upstream surface. In the hydrodynamic collapse regime, hotspots nucleate at the material interfaces, with void length-dependence in PV work, shock temperature, and the onset of self-sustaining chemistry. Driven by shock-induced deformation and HMX decomposition, the binder undergoes backbone chain scission followed by extensive aromatic-backbone cross-bonding, akin to a graphite to diamond transformation. These reactions act as heat sinks, suppressing deflagration and ultimately inhibiting hotspot growth and coalescence between crystals. The simulations further link the polymer's chemical response to the shock-to-detonation transition in polymer-bonded explosives.

infographic.key_insight: Polystyrene can intensify initial shock-induced heating at HMX pore interfaces, yet its subsequent heat-absorbing reactions suppress hotspot growth and coalescence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Explosive safety and initiation models should account for binder chemistry as well as pore geometry because early hotspot heating does not necessarily predict sustained reaction growth.
method: Reactive molecular dynamics of shock-driven void collapse in an HMX crystal–gap–crystal stack.
Polystyrene placed along the upstream crystal surface.
Characterization of void-length effects, hotspot evolution, and polymer reactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations show void-length dependence in pressure–volume work, shock temperature, and self-sustaining chemistry onset, while polymer chain scission and extensive aromatic–backbone cross-bonding absorb heat and inhibit hotspot growth.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports simulation evidence for a specific HMX–polystyrene geometry, so transferability to other binders and realistic pore networks requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Polymer-Mediated Hotspot Evolution in Shock-Induced Pore Collapse in 1,3,5,7-Tetranitro-1,3,5,7-tetrazocane (HMX)-based Explosives

title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation
authors: Ziqiao Meng, Rongsheng Chen, Zhi Zheng, Nikita Kazeev, Zhenkun Wang, Andrey Ustyuzhanin
abstract: Deep generative modeling has achieved remarkable progress in crystal generation. Given the rich symmetries inherent in crystalline structures, recent work has sought to explicitly incorporate space-group symmetry into generative models, enabling more effective exploration of novel symmetry templates. Yet introducing symmetry templates increases the combinatorial complexity of stoichiometric relationships between atomic species and crystallographic sites, while creating a fundamental tension between flexible exploration of discrete crystallographic templates and faithful realization of these templates as continuous three-dimensional structures. To address these challenges, we propose CrystalAR, a unified autoregressive framework that models Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures within a single generative sequence. Specifically, CrystalAR reformulates continuous coordinate generation as a symmetry-conditioned hierarchy of discrete spatial localization decisions, autoregressively refining the positions of all symmetry-inequivalent sites across resolution levels while jointly modeling their spatial configuration within each level. This discrete hierarchical formulation further enables constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations. As a result, CrystalAR retains strong symmetry-template generation capability while achieving competitive de novo generation performance and template-free crystal structure prediction (CSP) accuracy. These results suggest that symmetry-template generation can be retained alongside broadly competitive de novo generation performance and competitive CSP without reliance on symmetry templates retrieved from prior data, providing a promising alternative paradigm for symmetry-preserving crystal generation.

infographic.key_insight: CrystalAR unifies crystal symmetry templates and full 3D structures in one autoregressive sequence, preserving symmetry while exploring new crystal configurations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support computational materials discovery by generating crystals and predicting structures without retrieving symmetry templates from prior data.
method: Jointly generate Wyckoff symmetry templates and complete crystal structures.
Localize symmetry-inequivalent sites through hierarchical, symmetry-conditioned discrete spatial decisions.
Use constraint-aware search over both crystallographic templates and geometric realizations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports strong symmetry-template generation and competitive de novo generation and template-free crystal structure prediction, but provides no datasets or quantitative metrics.
infographic.watch_item: The computational cost and geometric precision of hierarchical spatial refinement and constraint-aware search require assessment.
infographic.paper_title: CrystalAR: Autoregressive Modeling for Symmetric Crystal Generation

title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion
authors: Valentin Munteanu, Alexander Hinderhofer, Dmitry Lapkin, Vladimir Starostin, Frank Schreiber
abstract: X-ray and neutron scattering are indispensable for structural characterization across condensed-matter physics and materials science. Yet, because scattering experiments generally record intensities without phase information, distinct structures can yield similar scattering patterns, rendering the corresponding inverse problems non-unique. This ambiguity can be reduced by combining complementary measurements, but their integration into machine-learning frameworks remains challenging. Here we introduce a modular framework for probabilistic multi-measurement analysis based on prior-amortized flow matching. Single-observation posterior estimators are trained separately for individual observation types or physical probes and combined only at inference time through a compositional sampler. This late fusion approach allows pretrained single-observation models to be reused without dedicated joint retraining. As a case in point, we consider reflectometry, which provides depth-resolved, nanometer-scale information about thin films and interfaces. Our single-observation demonstrations span X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry. In separate co-refinement studies, task-matched estimators enable homogeneous composition across multiple neutron contrasts and heterogeneous multimodal composition of X-ray and neutron measurements. Together, these results establish compositional flow matching as a modular approach to uncertainty-aware inversion and co-refinement, with potential applicability to other scattering problems in which multiple observations constrain a common physical structure while retaining measurement-specific parameters.

infographic.key_insight: Separately trained neural posterior estimators can be combined at inference time to constrain shared thin-film structure from complementary scattering measurements without joint retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This modular approach supports uncertainty-aware thin-film and interface characterization while enabling reuse of pretrained measurement-specific models.
method: Train single-observation posterior estimators using prior-amortized flow matching.
Fuse estimators at inference time through a compositional sampler.
Infer shared structural parameters while retaining measurement-specific parameters.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports single-observation demonstrations for X-ray, time-of-flight neutron and polarized neutron reflectometry, plus co-refinement across neutron contrasts and combined X-ray–neutron measurements.
infographic.watch_item: Composition relies on task-matched estimators; the abstract provides no quantitative accuracy or computational-cost benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: Compositional neural networks for multimodal X-ray and neutron scattering inversion

title: Methane and ethane adsorption on calcite surfaces: effects of surface morphology from molecular dynamics and 3D-RISM
authors: Felipe Silva Carvalho, Tyler Luchko, Zhen-Gang Wang
abstract: Understanding the adsorption of alkanes on mineral surfaces is important for industrial processes such as oil and gas recovery from shale reservoirs. Previous studies have examined the adsorption of functionalized and non-functionalized alkanes on calcite, as well as adsorption under confinement. However, real surfaces commonly exhibit defects that can influence adsorption behavior. In this work, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and the three-dimensional reference interaction site model (3D-RISM) are used to investigate the adsorption of methane and ethane on calcite surfaces with step defects. MD simulations were carried out with and without positional restraints to investigate the effects of carbonate reorientation. 3D-RISM calculations were performed on these structures and on energy-minimized configurations of the relaxed crystal. Both methods show adsorption enhanced at step defects relative to flat regions, with methane exhibiting higher excess adsorption than ethane. Carbonate reorientation at the relaxed step edges reduces the local density peaks at specific step sites in both methods, while the integrated excess adsorption from MD remains comparable to that of the restrained surface. 3D-RISM predicts lower maxima for the highest density peaks and larger excess adsorption than MD, but reproduces the spatial organization and overall adsorption trends at a fraction of the computational cost. These results highlight the importance of surface heterogeneity in fluid-mineral interactions and demonstrate that 3D-RISM is an efficient tool for semi-quantitative screening of adsorption across complex surface geometries

infographic.key_insight: Calcite step defects enhance methane and ethane adsorption relative to flat regions, with methane showing higher excess adsorption than ethane.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for mineral surface defects can improve adsorption assessments relevant to oil and gas recovery from shale reservoirs.
method: MD simulations of methane and ethane near stepped calcite surfaces.
Restrained and unrestrained MD to isolate carbonate reorientation effects.
3D-RISM calculations on simulated structures and energy-minimized relaxed configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Both methods predict step-enhanced adsorption; 3D-RISM reproduces spatial patterns and overall trends at lower computational cost, but predicts lower peak densities and greater excess adsorption than MD.
infographic.watch_item: Use 3D-RISM for semi-quantitative screening rather than precise adsorption estimates because its peak densities and integrated excess adsorption differ from MD.

title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations
authors: Ali Karatutlu, Timuçin Emre Tabaru, Umut Taylan, Zehra Gizem Mutlay, Doğukan Hazar Özbey, Okan Uslu
abstract: Silicon-on-insulator is mostly the main driving material system for the field of silicon photonics, including PICs, due to high index contrast and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes [1]. A recent example is silicon oxynitride-doped silicon [2] discovered recently by our group, offering to set a new position for the fields of silicon photonics with a precise control of refractive index from 2.1 to 2.5 together with the photosensitivity property at different wavelengths. In this study, we demonstrate that the synthesis of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be performed on a flexible substrate for the fabrication of Bragg gratings (BG) at low temperatures below 100 degrees Celsius that are emerging for advanced applications. Their use in preserving ultra-fast lasers inscribed micro-information has been demonstrated numerically and experimentally due to its multispectral reflection behaviour from the ultraviolet (UV) to the near-infrared (NIR) regions. The unique structural characteristics of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon were studied at the Si L, O K and N K edges using soft X-ray absorption studies. The quantum mechanical calculations provide the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, whereas the crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx was conducted using the particle swarm optimization method in combination with density functional theory (DFT).

infographic.key_insight: Silicon oxynitride-doped silicon enables laser-inscribed flexible Bragg gratings fabricated below 100 °C for multispectral authentication.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Low-temperature processing, photosensitivity, and refractive-index control from 2.1 to 2.5 offer a route to flexible photonic security features.
method: Synthesize silicon oxynitride-doped silicon films on flexible substrates and inscribe Bragg gratings with ultrafast lasers.
Probe local structure using soft X-ray absorption at the Si L, O K, and N K edges.
Investigate formation mechanisms with quantum calculations and predict bulk Si3N4−xOx structures using particle swarm optimization with DFT.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical and experimental demonstrations of micro-information preservation through multispectral reflection from UV to near-infrared wavelengths.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify authentication performance or durability under repeated bending and environmental exposure.
infographic.paper_title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations

title: Stabilization of Ferroelectric Domains via Interfacial Strain in HoFeO3- BaTiO3 Nanofiber Heterostructures for Enhanced Hybrid Energy Harvesting
authors: Smita Chaturvedi, Swathi Krishna, Shivshankar Jokare, Supriya Sahoo, Vikash Kushwaha, Priyank Shyam
abstract: Piezoelectric nanogenerators (PENGs) are an attractive platform for self-powered mechanical-energy harvesting, but their output is often limited by depolarization fields, charge leakage, and inefficient stress transfer to the active dipoles, particularly in polymer-dominated composites. Here we report HoFeO3-BaTiO3 (HFO-BTO) nanofiber heterostructures prepared by alternating sol-gel electrospinning, in which orthorhombic HoFeO3 (Pbnm) and tetragonal BaTiO3 (P4mm) coexist in intimate contact. Rietveld-refined X-ray diffraction, high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy indicate interfacial lattice distortion. Polarization-electric field loops show that the heterostructure retains a polarization comparable to that of BaTiO3 (16.39 vs 15.80 microcoulombs per square centimeter at zero field) while its switching-current maximum moves to a higher field (about 7 vs about 3.5 kilovolts per centimeter), consistent with strain-stabilized ferroelectric domains. When the nanofibers are encapsulated in polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) and excited under cyclic impact, the device produces a hybrid output: the piezoelectric response of the strained BaTiO3 is supplemented by a triboelectric contribution from contact electrification. The HFO-BTO device delivers open-circuit voltage peaks of about +6 volts and -8 volts and a power density of 24.31 microwatts per cubic centimeter at a 4.7 megaohm load. This is 2.4 times the value for an identically fabricated BaTiO3 device (10.00 microwatts per cubic centimeter) and 8.7 times that of the HoFeO3 device (2.78 microwatts per cubic centimeter). These results link interface-driven lattice distortion to improved electromechanical output and identify all-oxide nanofiber heterostructures as a promising route to lead-free energy harvesting.

infographic.key_insight: Interfacial lattice distortion in HoFeO3–BaTiO3 nanofibers is consistent with stabilized ferroelectric domains and enhanced hybrid piezoelectric–triboelectric energy harvesting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: All-oxide nanofiber heterostructures offer a lead-free route to improving mechanical-energy harvesters embedded in flexible PDMS.
method: Prepare HoFeO3–BaTiO3 heterostructures by alternating sol–gel electrospinning.
Probe crystal structure, interfaces, and polarization using refined XRD, HRTEM, Raman spectroscopy, and electrical measurements.
Encapsulate nanofibers in PDMS and evaluate cyclic-impact output against single-oxide devices.
infographic.evidence_signal: The heterostructure delivered 24.31 µW/cm³ at 4.7 MΩ—2.4× the BaTiO3 control—with comparable zero-field polarization and a switching-current peak shifted to a higher field.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify the separate piezoelectric and triboelectric contributions or report long-term cycling durability.
infographic.paper_title: Stabilization of Ferroelectric Domains via Interfacial Strain in HoFeO3- BaTiO3 Nanofiber Heterostructures for Enhanced Hybrid Energy Harvesting

title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
authors: Reza T Batley, Sourav Saha
abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

infographic.key_insight: Rectified-flow generation coupled with exact latent-space refinement enables concurrent optimization of printable bone-scaffold microstructures and their spatial arrangement.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework designs highly porous implants that closely match target bone mechanics under multiple loads, with potential applications in metal additive manufacturing.
method: Generate periodic lattice microstructures using a conditional rectified-flow model.
Refine latent designs using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities.
Jointly optimize unit-cell geometry and spatial assignment under mechanical and feature-size constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: All eight rabbit-benchmark refinements achieved under 1% error across six target moduli; human femoral designs reached 63% cortical porosity with compliance within 2% and 84% cancellous porosity with strain-energy deviations below 0.25%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational benchmarks but does not establish fabricated-scaffold performance or biological integration.
infographic.paper_title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement

title: MOFFieldBench: A Machine Learning Benchmark for Continuous Electronic Fields in Metal-Organic Frameworks
authors: Zhaolin Hu, Hehe Fan, Chenhao Rao, Wangyihan Guo, Meng Xu, Qiwei Yang
abstract: Machine-learning models for metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) predominantly rely on atomic structures, whereas electron-density (ED) and electrostatic-potential (ESP) fields remain underexplored as scalable learning representations. These continuous fields encode complementary spatial and electronic information relevant to structure-property relationships, particularly pore geometry and guest-framework interactions, but costly first-principles calculations, storage requirements and the scarcity of systematically aligned datasets limit their broader use. Here we introduce MOFFieldBench, a multimodal benchmark comprising approximately 46,000 MOFs with one-to-one aligned crystallographic structures, ED fields and ESP fields. A unified workflow integrates field generation, error-controlled compression and sparse point-cloud representation, supporting field reconstruction, prediction of 13 material properties, multimodal property prediction and pairwise cross-modal retrieval. ED and ESP provide competitive representations for pore geometry, adsorption and separation properties. Multimodal fusion improves several prediction tasks relative to the best unimodal reference, supporting complementary predictive roles for atomic structures and electronic fields. Learned ED reconstruction closely approximates first-principles reference densities, while predicted-density initialization reduces self-consistent-field calculation time by 13.59\% on average in paired tests. These results support electronic fields as practical, informative learning modalities and establish MOFFieldBench as a resource for studying representation choice, multimodal learning and electronic-field-driven MOF modelling.

infographic.key_insight: MOFFieldBench establishes electron-density and electrostatic-potential fields as complementary learning representations to atomic structures for metal-organic frameworks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Electronic-field learning can support MOF screening for adsorption and separation while providing initial densities that accelerate first-principles calculations.
method: Align crystallographic structures with electron-density and electrostatic-potential fields for approximately 46,000 MOFs.
Combine field generation, error-controlled compression and sparse point-cloud representations.
Benchmark field reconstruction, 13-property prediction, multimodal fusion and pairwise cross-modal retrieval.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multimodal fusion improves several prediction tasks over the best unimodal reference, and predicted-density initialization reduces self-consistent-field calculation time by 13.59% on average in paired tests.
infographic.watch_item: Generating reference electronic fields remains computationally costly, and the reported gains should not be assumed to generalize beyond the evaluated tasks and paired tests.
infographic.paper_title: MOFFieldBench: A Machine Learning Benchmark for Continuous Electronic Fields in Metal-Organic Frameworks

title: Paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$: complete one phonon Raman spectrum
authors: Taras Palasyuk, Dominik Kurzydłowski, Ashutosh S. Wadge, Rajmund Bacewicz, Madhavi H. Dalsaniya, Michał Wierzbicki
abstract: In this study we present a complete first-order Raman scattering spectrum of paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$- a material, where new type of spin texture induced by noncoplanar antiferromagnetic ordering below the Néel temperature ($T_N \approx 90$ K) gives rise to unconventional scenario of magnetism. Basic properties of all five phonon modes ($A_g$, $E_g$ and three $T_g$) predicted by the group theory have been successfully approached through polarization, excitation and temperature dependent measurements. In particular, the ever-missing phonon mode of $T_g$ symmetry has been unambiguously resolved in the room temperature Raman spectrum at approximately 107 cm$^{-1}$, just 1.5 cm$^{-1}$ higher in frequency compared to the $E_g$ mode. Density functional theory calculations reproduce the observed Raman-active phonon spectrum and support the assignment of all five first-order Raman modes, including the near-degeneracy of the $E_g$ and one of the $T_g$ vibrations. The calculations further reveal a dense manifold of low-energy antiferromagnetic spin configurations, separated from the ground state by only a few meV per formula unit. Furthermore, strong signals of inelastically scattered light from the paramagnetic (PM) phase of MnTe$_2$ were acquired with long wavelength excitations, i.e. 633 nm and 785 nm, revealing the $2A_g$ overtone at approx. 360 cm$^{-1}$. The enhanced absorption of the light in the near infrared range could be a putative reason behind the anomalous angular dependence of scattered intensity of the highest frequency $T_g$ phonon mode (183 cm$^{-1}$) measured in PM MnTe$_2$ with parallelly aligned polarizers. Finally, upon cooling just below the $T_N$, the measured properties of phonons remained basically unperturbed by the incipient long-range antiferromagnetic ordering.

infographic.key_insight: All five first-order Raman phonon modes of paramagnetic MnTe₂ were identified, including a previously unresolved T_g mode near 107 cm⁻¹.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The complete Raman-mode assignment provides a reference for spectroscopic characterization and validation of computational models of MnTe₂.
method: Polarization-, excitation-, and temperature-dependent Raman measurements
Density functional theory calculations of phonons and magnetic configurations
Group-theory-guided assignment of A_g, E_g, and three T_g modes
infographic.evidence_signal: DFT reproduced the observed Raman spectrum, supporting the assignment of a T_g mode only 1.5 cm⁻¹ above E_g; cooling just below T_N ≈ 90 K left phonon properties largely unchanged.
infographic.watch_item: Near-infrared absorption is only a proposed explanation for the anomalous angular intensity dependence of the 183 cm⁻¹ T_g mode.
infographic.paper_title: Paramagnetic phase of MnTe$_2$: complete one phonon Raman spectrum

title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
authors: Yuki K. Wakabayashi, Yui Ogawa
abstract: Self-driving laboratories accelerate materials exploration through autonomous closed-loop integration of synthesis, characterization, and next-experiment selection. However, characterization does not always directly provide the target property; measured spectra or images often require automated analysis to extract quantitative descriptors based on physically motivated assumptions and predefined criteria. Such procedures can fail for measurements outside these criteria, requiring a decision on whether a reliable value can be recovered or no numerical value should be reported. Here, we implemented an autonomous adaptive spectral-analysis agent using a large language model (LLM) to supervise a deterministic numerical-analysis routine. For each spectrum, the agent executes the predefined analysis script and assesses the result using the measured spectrum and fitting diagnostics. Valid results are accepted unchanged, recoverable failures are reanalyzed through bounded adjustments of predefined fitting parameters, and NaN (not a number) is returned when no scientifically defensible value can be obtained. We evaluated the workflow on optical transmittance spectra from 203 epitaxial beta-Ga2O3 films grown during a previously reported self-driving thin-film growth campaign. The predefined optical analysis script returned Urbach energy, an optical-quality metric, for 183 spectra and failed for 20. The agent retained those 183 values and evaluated 20 exception cases, recovering 16 through bounded parameter adjustments and returning NaN for 4 when the spectral evidence did not support a reliable Urbach tail. The audit records captured spectral features, parameter changes, and rationale for each decision. These results demonstrate autonomous scientific exception handling by an LLM agent while leaving quantitative property extraction to deterministic numerical analysis.

infographic.key_insight: An LLM agent recovered defensible Urbach-energy estimates from failed spectral analyses while preserving valid results and withholding unsupported values.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive exception handling can reduce manual intervention in self-driving laboratories while keeping quantitative property extraction deterministic.
method: Run a predefined numerical-analysis script on each optical transmittance spectrum.
Use an LLM agent to assess spectra and fitting diagnostics, accepting valid results unchanged.
Retry recoverable failures with bounded fitting-parameter adjustments; return NaN when evidence is insufficient.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 203 epitaxial β-Ga2O3 film spectra, the agent retained 183 baseline estimates, recovered 16 of 20 failures, and returned NaN for 4, with decisions documented in audit records.
infographic.watch_item: Evaluation was limited to one material system and measurement workflow; reliability on other spectra and fitting procedures remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous adaptive spectral analysis with an LLM agent for self-driving laboratories
